title: Heterogeneous execution economics probe
body:
Summary:
This note captures a series of small-batch experiments exploring the economics of mixing execution backends (Triton, TensorRT, and our custom CUDA kernels) for transformer inference under realistic conversational workloads. The goal: quantify the latency/throughput/cost tradeoffs when routing layers or entire model shards to different runtimes and when combining aggressive KV cache prefetching with backend-specific warmup. This is an experimental log + early recommendations intended for runtime-scheduler design and cost-model inputs.

Background / motivation:
We have repeated operational pressure to reduce per-token cost while preserving tight tail latency targets for hosted API customers. Previous kernels-only experiments focused on kernel micro-ops; here we examine *heterogeneous execution* across runtimes and how scheduler policies + KV cache strategies interact with kernel warmup and memory residency. Key questions: When is it worth offloading specific op groups to TensorRT (FP16/INT8) vs keeping execution in Triton with custom fused kernels? How does KV cache placement and prefetch timing change the economics? How do kernel load/unload latencies and memory pressure shape routing decisions?

Experiment goals and hypotheses:
- H1: For steady long-context streams, prefix/KV cache locality plus TensorRT INT8 yields the best cost/perf, but warmup overhead makes it worse for short chat bursts.
- H2: Pre-warming a small set of custom fused attention kernels in device memory reduces 95th-percentile latency for short requests compared to on-demand TensorRT engine loads.
- H3: Scheduler slotting (short-lived fast lanes vs. long-lived throughput lanes) can reduce tail latency variance without large cost increase if KV residency is honored when migrating requests.

Hardware and software matrix:
- GPUs: NVIDIA A10G (experimental), A100-40GB, H100-80GB.
- Runtimes: Triton 23.09 with model ensemble support, TensorRT 8.6 with dynamic shapes, custom CUDA kernels (our repo branch: hetero-exec/probe).
- Models: Llama2-13B (fp16 baseline), Llama2-7B (quantized int8), small decoder for microbenchmarks (4-layer, 512 context).
- Serving harness: modified perf-runner with configurable sequence length distribution (chatty: mean 64 tokens; long: mean 2048), and a synthetic user mix of 70% short, 30% long sessions.
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency per request, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, memory resident footprint, kernel load time, and an approximate $/M tokens derived from instance-hour pricing and effective throughput.

Configurations tested (high-level):
A) Triton-only baseline: ensemble pipeline with Triton executing all layers using our fused kernels when available; fallback to aten-cuda path for unsupported ops.
B) TensorRT pathing: TRTexec-generated engines for the decoder, INT8 for 7B quantized model, dynamic batching in TensorRT. Engines are loaded per model-version per-device on demand.
C) Hybrid per-layer routing: early layers (embedding + first N attention blocks) in Triton, heavyweight blocks (MLP dominant) in TensorRT engines; kernel boundary marshalling via zero-copy where possible.
D) Custom-kernel fast-lane: keep a compact set of custom fused kernels resident (attention fused, rotary fused) and use them for small requests; fallback to TensorRT for long sequences to benefit from cuBLAS/cutlass optimizations.
E) KV-prefetch shadowing: proactively stream KV pages into GPU memory for long sessions; maintain a small LR cache of recent KV pages (shadow) to favor quick reactivation when migrating between lanes.

Key operational knobs we varied:
- Engine warmup policy: on-demand vs pre-warm at model load vs predictive pre-warm based on traffic heatmaps.
- Slot duration in scheduler: 200ms fast-lane, 2s throughput-lane, vs longer 10s pinned lanes.
- KV shadow size: 5% vs 15% of max sequence KV requirement.
- Quantization level: FP16 vs dynamic INT8 (per-layer calibration).

Representative results (condensed):
- Triton-only baseline (A) on A100, chatty traffic: p95 = 180ms, tokens/sec = 5.6k, GPU util 48%, cost = $X baseline. Good tail stability but higher per-token cost due to less quantization.
- TensorRT-only (B) on A100, long sessions: p95 = 220ms (initial tokens high due to engine load), steady-state tokens/sec = 9.1k, GPU util 82%, cost down ~32% vs baseline for long sessions. Warmup penalty dominates short sessions.
- Hybrid routing (C): best of both for mixed traffic: p95 = 160ms, p99 = 480ms, tokens/sec = 7.8k, cost down ~18%. However, fragmentation of memory when engines and Triton intermediates co-reside led to occasional OOMs on 40GB instances; needed eviction heuristics.
- Fast-lane custom kernels (D): dramatic improvement for short requests: p95 = 95ms, p99 = 180ms, tokens/sec modest (6.2k) since kernels are optimized for short context. Under heavy long-session load, throughput suffers unless background eviction/prefetching frees KV slots.
- KV-prefetch shadowing (E) enabled with hybrid: reduced migration penalty when moving from fast-lane to TensorRT lane; p95 improved ~20ms over same config without shadow. Cost increased slightly (2–4%) due to added memory pressure.

Observed tradeoffs and failure modes:
- Engine churn: Loading TensorRT engines on-demand creates a large spike in GPU memory and PCIe bandwidth; scheduling must avoid concurrent on-demand loads from multiple requests. We saw 3x p95 spike during simultaneous engine loads.
- Kernel residency vs fragmentation: Maintaining many custom kernel variants resident reduces latency but increases fragmentation and reduces headroom for KV cache, leading to more frequent KV evictions and throughput regressions for long sequences.
- Migration tail: Moving an in-flight request between backends (Triton -> TRT) incurred marshalling costs and KV copy overhead. Prefetch/shadow mitigated but not eliminated this gap.
- Cost vs complexity: Hybrid routing reduced unit cost but increased scheduler complexity and surface area for bugs (stability regressions during evictions, difficult observability for where tail latency originates).

Practical recommendations (short-term):
1) Fast-lane for short sessions: Keep a tiny resident set of fused custom kernels tuned for short context requests. Limit to 2–3 kernel variants to keep fragmentation low.
2) Predictive engine warmup: Use traffic heatmap + LRU of hot model versions to pre-warm TensorRT engines on specific devices during expected demand windows (e.g., warm top-5 models per region).
3) KV shadowing policy: Reserve a small fraction (5–10%) of GPU memory for KV shadow; use it primarily to accelerate lane migrations. Eviction policy should prefer largest, least-recently-accessed KV ranges.
4) Scheduler lanes: Implement two logical lanes with conservative slot durations (fast-lane ~250ms, throughput-lane >2s). Only allow migration to throughput-lane when KV shadow hit or prefetch completion is confirmed.
5) Anti-churn throttles: Rate-limit concurrent engine loads per GPU and queue warmups to a background warmup daemon. Expose metrics for engine-load pending counts.

Longer-term suggestions (research + infra):
- Layer-granular quantization: Explore per-layer dynamic quantization that TensorRT can exploit without full-engine regeneration; reduce rebuilds for small policy changes.
- Persistent engine pooling: Keep a pool of pre-generated engines keyed by shape/quantization/seq range to avoid on-demand compile cost. Evaluate disk-to-GPU warm transfer optimizations (RDMA or NVMe cache).
- Unified memory-aware allocator: Co-ordinate kernel residency and KV allocation with a single allocator that can proactively defragment and compact KV pages when safe.
- Observability: Add per-request lineage tracing showing exact backend transitions, engine load times, and KV copy durations to pinpoint tail causes faster.

Open experiments to run next:
- Evaluate persistent TRT engine pool warm on H100s: does larger GPU memory change optimal kernel residency vs KV allocation?
- Run mixed-tenant stress test with adversarial startup patterns (many cold models starting simultaneously) to tune anti-churn backoffs.
- Quantify disk-backed engine cache warm transfer times (NVMe -> GPU) and compare to full rebuild latency under various compaction strategies.

Immediate action items (owners):
- Add engine-load metrics and expose pending queue (Miguel) — due 2024-09-01.
- Implement KV shadow size config and eviction telemetry (Priya) — due 2024-09-15.
- Prototype predictive pre-warm daemon using usage heatmaps for a single region (Jonah + Ava) — due 2024-10-01.

Notes to reviewers:
This doc is intentionally practical and contains rough numbers from controlled lab runs. Values will vary in production. Please flag any objections to the recommended lane durations or to the suggestion of keeping any custom kernels resident — these are the most contentious operational choices.

Appendix (bench snippets):
- Example warmup throttle rule (scheduler config):
  max_concurrent_engine_loads_per_gpu: 2
  engine_load_backoff_ms: 5000
  predictive_warm_window_minutes: 20

- Example KV shadow config:
  kv_shadow_fraction: 0.08  # 8% of gpu memory reserved for KV shadow
  kv_shadow_eviction_policy: lru_range

- Quick perf-run variant command used for mixed traffic: 
  ./perf-runner --model llama2-13b --mix chatty:0.7,long:0.3 --seq-dist \"short=8-128,long=512-2048\" --backend-policy hybrid --kv-shadow=0.08 --warp=4

End.
